## A FIRED BUILD CAN SAY HOW IT IS GOING, AND UNTIL NOW IT COULD NOT (2026-08-26)

**Run 40 fired correctly — `202 after 204.0s`, job `dce16075…`, 6 credits, the Worker's invocation over and the generation left in the container — and then produced no site, and NOTHING on the platform could say which link broke.** That is the finding. The fire is stage 2's hard half and it worked; what was missing was any way to observe the second half.

- **THREE FAILURES WITH THREE DIFFERENT FIXES PRODUCE THE SAME THREE OBSERVATIONS.** The delayed message never delivered · the container losing the work and the fallback failing · a resume looking and losing its claim. On every one the site serves the stand-in (**which it also does while a build is working perfectly**), the trace goes quiet, and `GET /api/site/build/<job>` answers a bare `pending`. An hour of watching separated none of them, and the two instruments that should have helped were themselves broken — the resume's recorder was never identified and its clock was a string, both fixed the same night.
- **THE MEASUREMENT IS `looks` AGAINST `due`, and it is the only pair that discriminates.** The resume record already counts the looks it has HAD; `looksDue` says how many the SCHEDULE owes by now. `looks 0 / due 0` is too early to say anything; **`looks 0 / due N` is a record the fire stored that nothing ever came back to** — which is delivery of a DELAYED message, the one link in this path nothing before stage 2 exercised. Immediate delivery is proven (the consumer ran the build); `delaySeconds` is new and untested. `looks << due` is messages arriving and losing their claim; `looks ≈ due` is a generation still running.
- **`looksDue` IS DERIVED FROM THE TWO CONSTANTS THAT DO THE SCHEDULING, and the test WALKS `resumeDecision` rather than restating a cadence.** A hand-written expectation drifts the first time either constant moves, and what it then reports is a healthy build as stalled — the exact inversion this is for. **The first interval is counted TWICE**, because the schedule spends it twice: the fire sends with `RESUME_FIRST_SECONDS` and the look that arrives then sees `looks === 0` and is given it AGAIN. Read off that expression, never remembered.
- **THE FLIGHT CARRIES COUNTERS AND THE SLUG AND NOTHING ELSE, and that is why it is a function rather than a spread.** The record holds the caller's own live access token and the whole design. `flightOf` is the only thing that ever shapes one, asserted as an exact key set AND by value on the response text — a key check passes on a field that happens to be named innocently, and a route reaching into the record itself is one edit from returning the token with it. Gated on the record's own uid, by the same rule as the result.
- **IT IS A COURTESY AND MAY NEVER CHANGE THE ANSWER.** The RESULT read answers 503 on a blip deliberately — reading it as pending polls for ever against a finished build — and the same blip on this strictly less important read must not take a healthy in-flight build down with it. A throw, a record that will not parse and a record from another version all keep the 202. **A build with no record is byte-identical to before**, so nothing that does not use the feature changed shape.
- **AND THE PROBE IS FREE, which is the whole point.** `scripts/build-flight.mjs` + `build flight` sign in with the repo's own secrets and make ONE authenticated GET — no model call, no container, no build, no Neon project, nothing billed. Another `build as owner` run is ~130 credits and could have been inconclusive for the third time. **It is pointed by hand at one job id in the workflow**, because it CONSUMES a finished result (that route is delete-on-read), so it must never be aimed at a build somebody is polling for.
- **TWO EXISTING GUARDS WENT RED ON A CORRECT CHANGE and both were the recorded own-goals.** One windowed the route at `at + 2200` BYTES and reported *"any signed-in caller can read any build's answer"* about an ownership check a few hundred bytes further down — never size a source-read window in bytes, ten-plus instances. The other sliced the pending branch to the first `;` after `if (!obj)`, a spelling that assumed a one-line branch and stopped meaning anything the moment the branch grew a body. Both re-anchored on properties, and the window's bound is now **asserted in both directions**, because a terminator that stops matching answers -1 and silently widens to the rest of the file — which is how a guard went quiet earlier in this same arc.
- 4298 tests, **7/7 mutations as expected** from a verified-green isolated baseline with a comment-only control that had to survive, and the tree proved byte-identical afterwards. **NOT PROVEN LIVE** — the next push runs the probe, and its answer is what says why run 40 produced no site.

## THE WORKER STOPS WAITING — THE BUILD FIRES ITS GENERATION AND ENDS (2026-08-25, owner's call)

**"But the worker should not just wait remember?"** Stage 1 moved the ten-minute call to the side with no clock and left the consumer holding the socket, which is the half its own entry called out in as many words: *"this does not yet raise the ceiling — it moves the call to where it can live."* This is the other half. The invocation that starts a build now fires the generation at the container, stores where the answer will be, and **returns 202 in seconds**; a later, short invocation reads it.

- **THE SEAM IS `deps.generate()`, AND IT IS THERE BECAUSE NOTHING ABOVE IT SPENDS.** Grepped rather than assumed: the only charge in `publishPages` is `settle`, which runs after `deps.publish`. So an invocation that returns at the generate call has taken nothing — which is what lets the resume charge exactly once without any charge to undo. Every other seam would have needed a refund.
- **AND `page-gen.mjs` NEEDED NO CHANGE AT ALL, which is the property that made this small.** `generateSitePages` already takes its model call as a PARAMETER with no try/catch around it, so the fire throws a sentinel and **the resume passes a `call` that hands back the stored answer** — the parse, the `stop_reason` check, the four token kinds and the pricing all run through the code the synchronous path uses. A resume that re-implemented the second half is a second billing path, and the first sign of it disagreeing would be a wrong invoice.
- **THE SENTINEL IS READ BEFORE ANY FAILURE HANDLING, and that ordering is money.** `retryHere` would read a fired generation as a failure that spent nothing and make the call AGAIN in the Worker — a second ten-minute generation running beside the one just started, on the path built to avoid holding one.
- **A FIRE THAT DOES NOT LAND FALLS THROUGH TO TODAY'S BEHAVIOUR.** An older container image has no `/model/start` and answers 404, and Cloudflare's image rollout is asynchronous — so for a minute or more after a deploy the previous image is still serving. Degrading there costs a build the new ceiling and loses nothing that worked before it.
- **THE HOP IS BOUNDED AT 20 SECONDS, NOT AT `callMs`.** It stores a job and returns; bounding it at the generation's own ceiling would hold this invocation for ten minutes on a container that is not going to answer, which is the bug being fixed.
- **THE LANE IS RECORDED, NEVER RECOMPUTED.** The answer lives in ONE container instance's memory, so a resume that recomputed `laneName(slug)` after a mid-build deploy would ask an instance that never had the work and be told `unknown` — which reads as a lost generation and is not one.
- **THE RECORD IS WRITTEN BEFORE THE MESSAGE IS SENT.** In the other order a resume arrives, finds nothing, reads that as a build that already finished, and abandons a generation still running — a build the customer paid the design call for and never gets.
- **`attachments` ARE DROPPED FROM THE RECORD, measured rather than guessed.** Up to 13.6MB of base64 per build, and `generateSitePages` touches them in exactly one place: building the request the resume's `call` discards unread.
- **AND A BUILD MAY ONLY FIRE WHEN THERE IS SOMETHING TO COME BACK WITH — `canFire` was an unconditional `true` for one edit, and that is a real bug found by reading the caller rather than by any test.** `enqueueSiteBuild` falls through and runs the build **INLINE** when the queue is unbound or a store write fails, and that path passes no job id — so a fire there starts a generation in a container nobody will ever return to and answers the customer with a `resuming` stage nothing downstream handles. The gate is all three of the id, the bucket and the queue, because each alone still leaves a way to fire with nowhere to store or schedule the resume. **The suite was green with it wrong**, which is the honest measure of what was holding it: nothing.

**AND THE OUTCOME WAS UNREACHABLE, WHICH IS WHAT MADE THE FEATURE UNFINISHED RATHER THAN MERELY UNPROVEN.** `awaitJobResult` reads the result key and **DELETES it** — right while one request waited for one answer, and wrong the moment a build answers twice: the 202 consumed the key, and the real answer landed minutes later where nobody was looking and stayed there for ever. So there was no way for anything — the harness, the client, the customer — to learn what happened.

- **`GET /api/site/build/<job>` IS THE SECOND READER, and it is why the result carries a uid.** The request that started the build is authorised by having started it; a reader minutes later is not, and a result body carries the site's slug, its cost and its notes. **An EMPTY stored uid never matches** — every result written before that field existed has none, and reading absence as a match would hand a stranger the first such answer they asked for.
- **A PENDING BUILD ANSWERS 202, NOT 404.** Still-being-written and never-existed want opposite responses from a client, and collapsing them is how a poll gives up on a build that is working.
- **AND `!out.uid ||` IS PROVABLY INERT TODAY, said out loud rather than left reading as protection it is not.** `authUser` ends `return user && user.id ? user : null`, so `bu.id` is always truthy in that route — and an empty stored uid therefore fails `out.uid !== bu.id` on its own. **So the driving case for it passes with the clause or without it**, which means asserting it there would be a presence standing in for a property, for the seventh time in this feature. It is kept because what makes it inert is a property of ANOTHER function one edit away from changing, and the test asserts THAT PREMISE — the day `authUser` stops requiring an id, the guard goes red and says to drive it. Same convention as `built.ok &&` and the `pressed` axis.
- **AND A BLIP IS NEITHER.** Reading a failed R2 look as `pending` would have a client poll for ever against a build that is already done.
- **BOTH LIVE HARNESSES FOLLOW IT NOW, and one of them would otherwise have been permanently red on its FIRST assertion.** `build smoke` asserts `status === 200`; a 202 is the ordinary answer now, so it collects the real one and continues — **a red check everybody knows about is a check nobody reads**, and this repo has paid for that once already. `build-as-owner` already watched the site and the trace rather than the response, so it survived by construction — but its step 5 would have printed `page=undefined cost=undefined` on a perfect build, which is every measurement the run exists for reading as absent. It collects the answer after its watch settles.
- **AND MY FIRST DRAFT OF THAT CALLED A FUNCTION THAT DOES NOT EXIST.** `siteIsLive` — a `ReferenceError` on the one path that reports a fired generation never answering. `node --check` passes it; only reading the file found it. The `vidRefN` class in a harness.

**AND THE LEDGER, WHICH IS THE HALF WORTH GETTING RIGHT TWICE.**

- **TWO THINGS STOP A DOUBLE CHARGE AND BOTH ARE NEEDED.** Concurrent: the record's own etag is a compare-and-set — `put(key, …, { onlyIf: { etagMatches } })` returns **null** when the precondition fails, verified against Cloudflare's docs before anything was designed on it, because a wrong belief there means the claim silently does not work and both invocations charge. **`delete()` has no `onlyIf`**, which is why the claim has to be the put. Sequential: the record carries what has already been taken.
- **THE POLL COMES FIRST AND THE CLAIM RECORDS WHAT WAS DECIDED.** Claiming before asking means the claim cannot say whether this look is about to spend, so a terminal one needs a SECOND write — and the gap between those two writes is exactly the window a mark exists to close. Asking first costs a `GET` on a container that is already ours.
- **`max_retries: 0` IS NOT THE GUARD, AND THAT IS THE POINT.** It makes a redelivery very unlikely and it is a CONFIG one edit from changing, weighed in its own comment as a money decision rather than a guarantee. A record whose `pages` is marked is refused outright.
- **THE RECORD GOES LAST.** Deleted before the work, a redelivery finds nothing, reads it as a finished resume, and the build is lost with its generation still running.

**FOUR OF FIFTEEN MUTANTS SURVIVED THE FIRST SWEEP, ALL MINE, AND ALL ONE CLASS: A PRESENCE STANDING IN FOR A PROPERTY.**

- **`if (false && alreadyCharged(stored, "pages"))` STILL CONTAINS THAT CALL**, so a `match` for it passed with the double-charge guard switched off. The whole condition is asserted now, and that it RETURNS — a check that runs and falls through is decoration.
- **THE WAIT/TERMINAL MARK WAS COMPARED BY INDEX, and both arms of one ternary are after the test that chooses between them.** So the mutant that marks a WAIT survived — and that one stalls a build silently: the next look refuses, and the generation sits finished and unread. The two arms are read apart now.
- **`const poll = null; const pollLater = await askContainerResult(…)` KEPT EVERY ORDERING INDEX IN PLACE** and decided on nothing. The name the poll wrote must be the name the decision reads.
- **`lastIndexOf` MADE THE DELETE CHECK BLIND TO A DELETE ADDED EARLIER.** Every delete is checked against the window now, rather than the last one.
- **AND THE SAME CLASS BIT ME TWICE MORE EARLIER IN THE SAME ARC** — a `no-cap` mutant that left the cap as a dead line, and a `retryHere` witness built on **the one message the two implementations agree on** ("timed out" is not "timeout"). Six instances in one feature; it is the own-goal to look for first.
- **MY OWN NEW GUARD ALSO HIT THE FLAT-BRACE-SCAN MISTAKE ON ITS FIRST RUN.** `buildAndPublishPages` is ~1,200 lines of template literals, JSON payloads and regexes, so a counter treating every `{` alike closed hundreds of lines early and reported the feature missing from the function that carries it. **The fifth recorded instance**, in a guard written the same hour. Bounded by the next top-level declaration, which a string cannot fake — with a floor on the window's own length, since a terminator that stopped matching would make every absence check below it vacuous.

**SEVEN EXISTING GUARDS WENT RED ON A CORRECT CHANGE AND EVERY ONE WAS PINNED TO A SPELLING.** Four to the inline `buildAndPublishPages(env, {` literal, which became a VARIABLE because the resume has to store the arguments — and one object built once cannot drift from what was run. One scan read `[^)]*\)` for a container lane and **could not see a bare identifier at all**, so the resume's own call dropped out silently; read by depth now, which is what makes its total check meaningful. One asserted **exactly one** function carries `callBuilderModel`'s signature — true of the day it was written and false the moment an honest second drop-in existed; resolved per enclosing function, with ambiguity failing loudly rather than picking one. And `budgetStage` went red on the new `fired` mark, which is a derived guard doing exactly its job.

- **AND ONE PROCESS FAILURE WORTH KEEPING: A KILLED SWEEP LEFT A LIVE MUTANT IN THE TREE.** My own shell timed out at ten minutes against a seventeen-minute sweep, so the `finally` never ran. **The sidecar is the only mechanism that survives a process that never runs a handler**, and it is what found it. Never commit while a sweep is running, and repair from the sidecar before believing any baseline.
- **AND THEN THE OTHER ONE: TWO SWEEPS RACED ON ONE TREE, and the tell was the LOG LOSING A LINE IT HAD ALREADY PRINTED.** A `nohup … &` inside a backgrounded wrapper looked dead — its log was zero bytes — so I started a second run, and the first had in fact survived: `tee` truncated the file on open and both processes then wrote to it. **Every result from that run proved nothing**, which is this repo's own recorded rule about a sweep whose isolation was violated. Killed **by PID** — `pkill -f "sweep.py"` matches the wrapper's own command line and takes the shell down with it, ten recorded instances — the tree rebuilt, proved byte-identical to the source, re-verified green, and re-run once. **A log that goes backwards is the signature; check for a second writer before reading the result.**

**AND THEN THE THIRD CONSUMER — THE CUSTOMER'S OWN BROWSER — WHICH WOULD HAVE BEEN TOLD A LIE.** A 202 is `r.ok`, carries a `slug` and no `error`, so it satisfies `public/chat.js`'s success gate exactly; `d.page` is absent, so `built` reads TRUE. The browser rendered **"✅ Built “X”. Tell me what to change."** over a site whose pages were still being written, and then invited a revise against a build still in flight. **A success that did not happen, which is worse than a failure that did.**

- **THE CLIENT FOLLOWS THE JOB, and the answer it collects IS the POST's own, byte for byte** — the result route replays the stored status, content-type and body, so every branch below the follow runs exactly as it always has. That is what makes this a follow rather than a second reader of a different shape, and it is why the customer sees the finished site without sending anything.
- **THREE OUTCOMES, NOT TWO.** A build that fired and had not answered by the time the follow stopped is neither built nor failed. **The recording still runs on that path** — the slug is CLAIMED, so a project that forgets it sends the next message as a fresh first build against a name it already owns and gets a 409 it cannot act on.
- **THE HONEST SENTENCE IS THE SERVER'S OWN (`d.msg`).** A second copy in the client is a second thing that can disagree with the route about what just happened.
- **A PENDING ANSWER IS NOT A FAILURE AND A RUN OF UNREADABLE ONES IS.** The route answers 503 both for a bucket blip and for a stored answer that will not parse; polling for ever against the second is worse than saying so, and treating one blip as the second abandons a build that is fine.

**AND THE RESULT ROUTE WAS DEAD ON ARRIVAL — `json is not defined`, five times, in a route the client and both live harnesses depend on.** There is no `json()` helper in `worker.js` scope; the convention is `Response.json(body, { status })`. **`node --check` passes it, esbuild bundles it, and all 4,252 tests were green**, because every guard on it was a source-read and a source-read cannot see a name that is not in scope. The `vidRefN` / `du.id` class again.

- **IT WAS INVISIBLE BECAUSE NOTHING CALLED IT.** `client-routes.test.mjs` drives only the routes the app actually uses, so the route was unreachable-by-any-test until the client learned to follow a 202 — **the same shape as the feature being dead, one layer out.** The client change is what exposed it, which is an argument for wiring the last consumer rather than leaving it for later.
- **SO EVERY BRANCH IS DRIVEN NOW, not read**: a route with six exits and one driven exit is five untested returns. GoTrue stubbed, R2 faked — the 401, the malformed id (which must never reach the store), the pending 202, a read that THREW, the owner's own answer replayed verbatim, and both refusals (a stranger, and a result written before the field existed).
- **AND FIXING IT TURNED TWO OF MY OWN GUARDS RED, both pinned to the `json(…, 503)` spelling** — a guard going red against its own fix. Re-anchored on the status as a NUMBER, scoped to its own return statement so a sibling branch cannot satisfy it.
- **PLUS ONE MORE SPELLING-PIN IN `wiring.test.mjs`**, which held `siteFinishBuild(origin, (built ? '✅ ' : '⚠️ ') …, buildWhy(d))` character for character — so lifting the reply into a `const` to add the third outcome failed a test about word order. Its two real properties are asserted apart now.
- **AND MY OWN NEW CLIENT GUARD MATCHED THE WRONG OCCURRENCE.** `followBuildJob` is declared above `reactSend` and has its own `if (r.status === 202)`, so a bare `indexOf` found the FOLLOWER's line, read its `continue` as an early return, and reported a fault in correct code. Scoped to the POST now — the `confirmSubmitter` trap, which is a wrong-occurrence match rather than a wrong pattern.
- **AND ONE OF MY OWN DRIVING FIXTURES PASSED FOR THE WRONG REASON — caught by reasoning about it BEFORE reading the sweep, which is the only reason it did not become a survivor hunted in the wrong place.** The malformed-job-id case asked for `/api/site/build/../../etc/passwd`, and **`new Request()` NORMALISES that to `/api/etc/passwd`** — a path matching no route at all. So it answered 404 from the bottom of the router, `isJobId` was never consulted, and "it never reached the store" was true trivially. **A green assertion sitting over a check it does not exercise**, which is the vacuous-pass shape this file records against negative assertions, arriving in a positive one. Three cases now — a plainly wrong id, an id one character short, and an **encoded** traversal that survives normalisation — each asserting **first** that the fixture still reaches the route.
- **AND THE SWEEP CONFIRMED THAT DIAGNOSIS RATHER THAN DISCOVERING IT: `route-no-jobid` SURVIVED, exactly as predicted before the result was read.** That is the useful shape — a survivor whose cause is already known costs nothing, where the same survivor found cold costs a hunt through a check that is fine. Re-run against the corrected fixtures it dies, and a second mutant now holds the premise the inert clause rests on.
- 4281 tests (+24 in `test/build-resume-wiring.test.mjs` — the wire and, now, the route's own branches driven), `site build` **246/246** against the real container, **18/18 mutations as expected across four sweeps** from verified-green isolated baselines, each with a comment-only control that had to survive — after two survivors were closed and re-proven, one of them predicted before its result was read. **NOT PROVEN LIVE**: no build has fired yet, and what a unit suite structurally cannot show is a real container holding a real generation across two real invocations.

## RUN 39: THE FLAG I ADDED TO READ A DEAD BUILD DIED WITH THE BUILD (2026-08-25)

**`northgroup-5`, bought specifically to settle whether a Cloudflare container can reach api.x.ai, and it answered nothing — because the measurement rode on a return value that a thrown build never produces.** `done: true, ok: false, total_ms: 780,504`, and the `pages` mark came back **`{ms: 608372, buildMs: 0, credits: 0}` with neither `genTried` nor `genVia`** on the one run that existed to read them.

- **THE CAUSE IS FOUR LINES APART IN ONE FUNCTION.** The route declares `let pages = { page: "placeholder", …, cost: 0, buildMs: 0 }` and then `pages = await buildAndPublishPages(...)` — **an assignment that only happens when the await RESOLVES.** Generation was aborted at the budget, that function threw, the catch below set `stage`/`error` on the literal, and every field the build computed went with the stack. `{buildMs: 0, credits: 0}` IS that literal, untouched, which is how the row identifies itself.
- **SO THE FIX FOR RUN 38 REPEATED RUN 38'S OWN MISTAKE ONE LAYER IN.** The measurement moved from **the response** (destroyed by the ~285s edge reset, eleven times) to **the return value** (destroyed by a throw) — and was unreadable on precisely the builds it was built for, twice over. **A thing that has to answer when the build does not cannot live inside the build**, which is the rule `raceDeadline` already established here in as many words when `rec`/`tr`/`budget` had to be hoisted for exactly this reason. I had that lesson written down in this file and did not apply it.
- **`genPath` IS THE CALLER'S OBJECT NOW, hoisted beside the placeholder literal and passed in as `genPathOut`.** A mutable object is written through by the closure rather than returned, so the route reads it whether the build returned or threw. The mark reads `genPath` directly and never `pages`.
- **AND THE GUARD WENT RED ON THE FIX, pinned to `pages.genVia === "container"` — the exact spelling of the bug.** Re-anchored on the property, plus an ORDERING assertion (the route must declare it between the literal and the call), which is the half that cannot be satisfied by moving the declaration back inside.
- **WHAT RUN 39 DID ESTABLISH, and it is not nothing.** Design **168,437ms** against run 38's 181,636, so `capMs` handed generation **607,868ms** — 12 seconds more rope than run 38's 595,900 — and it was cut at **608,372ms** anyway. **Five samples of this CRM brief: 333,716 · 340,277 · 595,900 (cut) · 608,372 (cut) · 619,822.** Two consecutive cuts at the ceiling now, which moves "unlucky draw" toward "this brief does not fit", and confirms that shortening the design call is not the lever — 13 seconds bought nothing.
- **COST: 6 credits (211 → 205), the design settlement.** Generation charges after publish, so a build that never publishes charges nothing for it. `buildFloor` and the charge-after-publish rule both behaved exactly as designed.
- **THE CONTAINER QUESTION IS STILL UNANSWERED AND IS NOW THE ONLY THING BLOCKING STAGE 2.** If egress is blocked, moving the WAIT is building on sand — the container would hold a call it can never make.
- 4213 tests, **4/4 mutations as expected** from a verified-green isolated baseline with a comment-only control that survived — including the run-39 bug restored exactly (`genPath` back inside the build), and one re-run honestly after my first pattern never applied.

## RUN 38 DIED AT THE BUDGET, AND ITS ROW COULD NOT SAY WHERE THE CALL WAS MADE (2026-08-25)

**`northgroup-4` never published — `done: true, ok: false, at: "pages", total_ms: 780,495` against a `BUILD_BUDGET_MS` of 780,000.** The whole-build deadline fired, to the half-second, and the site is still serving the 820-byte early stand-in with a 200 at every address it does not have.

- **THERE IS NO `img` MARK AT ALL, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE DIAGNOSIS.** Each mark is written at the START of the step it names, so `img` is what CLOSES generation — a row with `gen` followed directly by `pages` is a build whose generation call never returned. `pages` carries **595,900ms**, which is `capMs` handing generation whatever was left after a **181,636ms** design call, and it needed more.
- **FOUR SAMPLES OF ONE BRIEF NOW, AND THEY ARE BIMODAL: 333,716 (run 37) · 340,277 (run 36) · 595,900 cut (run 38) · 619,822 (run 35).** Two fast, two slow. On a slow draw, design 181k + generation 620k + the ~185k tail is **~986k — past the consumer's fifteen minutes entirely**, so this brief cannot be made to fit by moving the call. That is what stage 2 is for, and the entry above says in as many words that stage 1 does not raise the ceiling.
- **AND THE RUN COULD NOT ANSWER THE ONE QUESTION IT WAS FOR.** `out.via` is set when the container ANSWERS, and it is read at the `img` mark and on the response — so a build cut off mid-generation records nothing about which side held the call, and the response is destroyed by the ~285s edge reset anyway (eleventh instance; every run from 35 to 38). **The measurement lived in the two places a dead build never reaches.**
- **`genTried` IS THE HALF A DEAD BUILD STILL HAS.** It is set BEFORE the fetch rather than after it, and rides on the `pages` mark, which run 38 proves is written whether a build succeeds or is killed. With both flags the three cases separate, and the third is the one that could not be expressed: `tried` + `via=container` is the container holding it; `tried` + `via=worker` is a refusal fast enough to fall back, which is what a blocked egress looks like from here; **`tried` with NO `via` is a hop that never came back — which is itself evidence the container REACHED a provider, since a refusal is milliseconds and not minutes.**
- **AS NUMBERS, because `makeTrace` takes only finite numbers** — deliberately, so a connection string can never reach a trace by accident — and drops everything else silently.
- **AND THE WATCH READS `pages` FIRST, `img` ONLY AS THE FALLBACK.** Anchored on `img` alone it prints nothing for exactly the builds worth reading.

**THREE OF MY OWN GUARDS THEN WENT RED ON A CORRECT CHANGE, AND ALL THREE ARE THIS FILE'S RECORDED OWN-GOALS.**

- **TWO WERE BYTE-SIZED WINDOWS MY OWN COMMENT OUTRAN** — `tr.at("pages"` sliced `+ 700` in `publish-pages.test.mjs` and again in `trace.test.mjs`, both reporting that the entry "stopped deriving its timings" about an entry that derives them perfectly. Bounded by the entry's own `]));` now. **Never size a source-read window in bytes** — the rule is already written down here and this is the tenth-plus instance.
- **THE THIRD WAS MEASURING SOMETHING ELSE ENTIRELY, AND THAT IS THE USEFUL FINDING.** `worker-imports.test.mjs` asserted `kept > 0.45` on the comment blanker's output — and a whole-line comment contributes its full length to the denominator and nothing to the numerator, so **what it really asserted is "worker.js is less than 55% comments by character"**. This repo documents its reasoning in comments as policy, so that threshold falls on every documented change and eventually goes red on one that is entirely correct. It hit **exactly 45.0%** on a change that added no code to the serve path at all. **A guard whose threshold erodes as the codebase gets better is a false alarm with a countdown on it.**
  - **REPLACED WITH THE PROPERTY: every top-level declaration survives byte for byte at its own line.** That is the recorded failure stated directly — a runaway swallowing 2,592 lines of the serve path swallows dozens of declarations with it — and its count moves with the CODE rather than with the prose around it.
  - **A LINE-CARRIES-NO-MARKER RULE WAS TRIED FIRST AND IS WRONG, recorded because it looks right**: the middle lines of a block comment carry no `//`, no `/*` and no `*/` either, so it reported **1,058 lines eaten** against a correct blanker, first hit being the second line of a JSDoc header.
  - **PROVED TO STILL FIRE ON THE FAILURE IT EXISTS FOR**: blanking block comments before line comments — the real 2026-08-13 runaway, where a `//` whose text contains `/*` opens a match that eats the serve path — goes red on 3 checks.
- **AND ONE OF MY MUTANTS WAS INERT AND REPORTED A GAP THAT WAS NOT THERE.** `const blank = (src) => (src + "")._IDENT_ || src` followed by `.replace(...)` parses as `undefined || src.replace(...).replace(...)`, because `||` binds looser than `.` — so the blanker still ran and "SURVIVED" meant nothing. Re-run as a true identity it is caught. **Umpteenth recorded instance, and the reason a survivor is never believed until the mutation is shown to have changed behaviour.**
- 4213 tests, **11/11 mutations as expected** across two sweeps from verified-green isolated baselines, with a comment-only control that had to survive — including the ordering one re-run honestly, since deleting a line and MOVING it are not the same mutation and only the second tests an ordering assertion.

## THE TEN-MINUTE CALL MOVES TO THE SIDE WITH NO CLOCK (2026-08-25, owner's call)

**"that 15 min cap on workers paid, should be an issue if build takes 1 hour to make."** Page generation now runs in the CONTAINER. A queue consumer is guaranteed **fifteen minutes and that is a hard cap**; a container has *"no fixed maximum runtime"* (Cloudflare's words) and is bounded by an IDLE timeout instead.

- **THE MARGIN IS THE FINDING, AND IT IS TWO MINUTES.** Generation alone: run 38 **595,405ms**, run 35 619,822ms, run 36 340,277ms, run 37 333,716ms. Whole builds are 10m31s, 11m10s — against fifteen. So the longest step of every build has been running with two to five minutes of headroom against a ceiling that **stops the isolate outright**, and a stopped isolate publishes no fallback, logs no reason and answers nobody.
- **THE WORKER STILL BUILDS THE REQUEST, AND THAT SPLIT WAS FORCED RATHER THAN CHOSEN.** `pagesRequest` reaches fifteen modules and ~1MB of prompt machinery, **three of them at the repo ROOT** and outside `builder/`'s Docker build context where `COPY ../` is not legal. So the prompt tier cannot cross without a second copy of a ~36,000-token prompt, which is two things that drift. What crosses is the finished request; what happens in the container is the WAIT.
- **THE CALLER IS A PARAMETER, NOT A SECOND FUNCTION, and the parse is why.** `stop_reason`, the tool_use extraction, the four token kinds and the `model` stamped on the usage are the half that decides what a build is CHARGED — a second copy reachable only from the build path is two things that drift **on the money path**, invisible until a bill is wrong. One line varies; everything either side is shared by construction. The signature is `callBuilderModel`'s exactly, so a caller that ignores `keys` (the container has its own) is still a drop-in.
- **ONLY THE BUILD. The two edit lanes keep making it in the Worker** — they run on the HTTP path, they write a page or two rather than a site, and an extra hop there is a new failure mode bought for nothing. Asserted in both directions, because a lane silently gaining the hop is a new fault on the CHEAP path.
- **THE FALLBACK EXISTS BECAUSE ONE THING IS UNPROVEN AND IT IS NOT SMALL: whether a Cloudflare container can reach api.x.ai has never been observed.** Every check of `/model` so far refuses BY NAME before a request is made, precisely so it can run on every push without spending — so the first real build against this is also the first evidence, and a build is the one thing this platform cannot afford to spend twice. When the container reached NO provider, the Worker makes the call itself and the build finishes.
- **`retryHere` OWNS THE ONE QUESTION — WAS MONEY SPENT — AND EACH REFUSAL IS A FACT.** A numeric `status` is a provider's own answer, so the tokens are gone and repeating it also replaces a message the customer can act on with a second identical failure. A TIMEOUT has no status and may have spent everything, and retrying is a second ten-minute wait stacked on the first — **which is the exact clock this change exists to get under.** Everything else means no request was ever made: a key the container was not given, egress refusing the provider, a container answering something that is not a model answer. **THE ONE CASE IT GETS WRONG IS STATED**: a container that got an answer and failed while sending it back is retried and pays twice — bounded at one extra call, against a build that otherwise fails outright on a hiccup.
- **THE ERROR SHAPE IS RE-THROWN, NOT FLATTENED.** `upstreamKind` parses `detail` for the provider's error type and the one sentence that names an empty account; the route reports `upstream` as *"the numeric status from the model API and nothing else"*; `isCallTimeout` reads `e.name`. A container-side failure losing any of the three is a real 429 — retry in a minute — wearing a container fault. **The two sides spell the class differently on purpose**: `/model` answers a JSON `kind` (a `name` on a plain object would read as the error's own) and an Error carries `name`.
- **THE BODY CAP WOULD HAVE SWITCHED THE FEATURE OFF FOR EVERY ATTACHMENT BUILD, SILENTLY, AND ONLY MEASURING FOUND IT.** `/model` shared `MAX_BODY` with `/build` — **4MB**, fine for a bare page request (**34,763 characters**, measured) and far under what an attachment carries: `site-context.mjs` allows **13,981,096** characters of base64 blocks plus 240,000 of text, so a worst case is **13.6MB**. It would have 413'd, the hop would have read "no provider was reached", `retryHere` would correctly have made the call in the Worker — so **every build with a picture or a price list attached would quietly go back to running its ten-minute call on the capped side, which is the build most likely to need the time.** It would have looked exactly like the feature working. `MAX_MODEL_BODY` is 16MB and the guard **derives the worst case from `site-context.mjs`'s own constants**, so a raised attachment cap goes red rather than silently reopening this.
- **THE MEASUREMENT RIDES ON THE TRACE AS WELL AS THE RESPONSE, and that is not belt-and-braces.** A build that used the container and one that fell back produce the same pages, the same cost and the same site — so `genVia` is the ONLY observable difference. And **the response is the thing this platform keeps losing**: the edge resets a build's socket at ~285s, eleven recorded times, and runs 35 to 38 all finished with nobody holding the answer. So it is also a trace mark — **as a NUMBER**, because `makeTrace` takes only finite numbers (deliberately, so a connection string can never reach a trace by accident) and drops everything else **silently**.
- **THE LANE IS THE SLUG'S OWN**, so generation and the compile that follows land in the same instance; two lanes would be two containers per build and the second would be cold. **The container is now first touched at `gen` rather than at `compile`** — the same one cold start, ~10 minutes earlier, well inside `MAX_BUSY_HOLD_MS`'s thirty.
- **SEVEN GUARDS WENT RED ON A CORRECT CHANGE AND EVERY ONE WAS PINNED TO A SPELLING.** Three to the literal `callBuilderModel(` — the FOURTH re-anchor of that pair, resolved through `providerSend` now rather than spelled. One to the LAST argument of `genPages(...)`, which is a fact about an argument LIST (depth-aware now, because `keysFrom(env)` is the first argument and a flat scan stops at its paren — the **fifth** time this repo has needed one). Three to `mark?.("img")` with its closing paren, fixed with the `[,)]` trick this file already records for exactly this. And **one to a 1,200-byte source window** outrun by my own comment — in a guard whose neighbouring comment already records it being re-anchored once for a different spelling.
- **TWO SWEEP SURVIVORS, BOTH MINE, AND BOTH THE RECORDED SHAPES.** Deleting the line that puts the provider's status on the re-thrown error **SURVIVED**, because the guard asked whether the word `status` appeared anywhere in the function and it does, three times, for other reasons — **a presence standing in for a property, in the guard written for it.** And `await call(...)` reverted to `await callBuilderModel(...)` survived every source-read: the parameter stays declared, documented and passed, the build path still builds its container caller and hands it over, `providerSend` resolves the send and is satisfied — **and every generation runs in the Worker exactly as before.** Only DRIVING it can see that, so it is driven, with a second half asserting no request went out from here (the default is a real provider fetch, so one appearing means the parameter was bypassed rather than used).
- 4211 tests (+27), **20/20 mutations as expected** across four sweeps from verified-green isolated baselines, each with a comment-only control that had to survive — after the two survivors above were closed and re-proven. **NOT PROVEN LIVE, AND THE WHOLE POINT IS WHAT THE FIRST BUILD MEASURES**: `genVia: "container"` says egress works and the ten-minute call is off the capped side; `genVia: "worker"` says the container could not reach the provider and names why in the log. Either way the build finishes.
- **AND THE ONE THING ABOUT THIS HOP NOBODY HAS MEASURED, NAMED RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE DISCOVERED: how long a Worker may hold a fetch to its own container.** `CONTAINER_CALL_MS` allows an hour and the compile hop's longest observed run is **103,352ms**; generation asks for up to six times that. If there is a shorter undocumented ceiling, the hop times out — and a timeout is the one failure `retryHere` refuses to retry, so the build ends there rather than falling back. **Not worse in kind than before** (the same wait was previously the Worker's own `AbortSignal` on the model call) and it is a second place a timeout can come from, so the message names WHICH bound and its number: `AbortSignal.timeout` says only "the operation was aborted", and a hop giving up at 10.5 minutes and a provider hanging for ten would otherwise arrive as one sentence.
- **THE HALF THAT IS NOT DONE, STATED: the Worker still WAITS.** The call is on the side with no clock and the consumer holding the socket is still on the side with fifteen minutes, so **this does not yet raise the ceiling** — it moves the call to where it can live and makes the second half a change to WHERE THE WAIT HAPPENS rather than to who makes the call. That second half is a re-enqueue with `delaySeconds` (verified against Cloudflare's docs: `send(msg, {delaySeconds})` and `msg.retry({delaySeconds})`, max 24 hours) plus a resume record, and it touches the ledger — the deposit and `schemaSettlement` must each happen once across two consumer invocations — which is why it is its own change rather than appended here.

## EVERY BUILD GETS ITS OWN CONTAINER, AND THE NUMBER THAT DECIDES IT WAS NOT THE CONTAINER'S (2026-08-25, owner's call)

**"Inifinite containers dude, everytime a user types to make something it automatically creates a container."** The five fixed lanes are gone: `laneName(key)` answers one name per key, so two builds only ever queue behind each other when they are two builds of ONE site. `BUILD_LANES` and `buildLane` are deleted; all eight `laneName(...)` call sites are unchanged and become correct by construction.

- **THE STATED REASON FOR BUCKETING WAS HALF TRUE AND THE CONCLUSION WAS WRONG.** The entry below it says what Cloudflare does past `max_instances` is *"documented on neither container page, and the client library has no knowledge of the limit at all"* — the literal half is right, `max_instances` really does appear nowhere in `@cloudflare/containers`. But the library **recognises the ceiling by name**: `NO_CONTAINER_INSTANCE_ERROR = 'there is no container instance that can be provided to this durable object'` → 503, and `RATE_LIMITED_ERROR = 'you are requesting too many containers per second'` → 429, handled in three places. So the boundary is not unpredictable — it is two named errors with two distinct statuses, and hashing into five lanes to keep it unreachable bought nothing.
- **AND FIVE WAS 300x LOW, measured against Cloudflare's own figures rather than guessed.** An account may run 6 TiB of concurrent memory; `standard-1` is 4 GiB, so **memory binds first at 1,536 instances** — which is what their changelog means by *"over 1,500 instances of the standard-1 instance type concurrently"*. Billing is per active 10ms with **no charge for idle or reserved capacity**, so unused ceiling costs nothing.
- **THE WAIT WAS NEVER THE CONTAINER STARTING, and that is what made the bucketing expensive rather than merely cautious.** Measured 2026-08-25: a cold start is **2,453ms against 176ms warm**, on a ten-minute build. What a customer felt was QUEUEING behind somebody else's build — over five lanes two simultaneous builds collided about one time in five, six collided always, and a collision meant waiting out the whole build in front.
- **THE QUEUE IS WHAT ACTUALLY BINDS, NOT THE CONTAINER — and raising only the container would have been ENTIRELY INERT.** A queued build starts when a *consumer invocation* is free, so `max_concurrency: 5` on the `site-builds` consumer means five builds at a time whatever the container allows: containers plentiful, platform unchanged, every test green. **The wiring layer this repo has recorded twelve dead features in, arriving in a number rather than in a call site.** Found by reading the config the container line sits in, not by a test.
- **250 IS CLOUDFLARE'S DOCUMENTED MAXIMUM for a push consumer, so it is a ceiling rather than a choice**, and checking it mattered: a value above it is not a slower platform, it is **a config the deploy REFUSES**, which ships nothing at all — the failure that lost three merges on 2026-08-07. `SiteBuildContainer` is 1000 and `GameBuildContainer` 300 (sum 1300, under the 1,536 account ceiling), so the container pool can never be what refuses a queued build. That gap matters because `max_retries` is deliberately 0: a `NO_CONTAINER_INSTANCE_ERROR` would end a customer's build outright rather than wait for a slot. **The gap is used rather than decorative** — the cheap-edit spine drives the same container class from the request path and never touches this queue.
- **THE PLAIN BRANCH EXISTS FOR A DASHBOARD, and its bound was wrong by twelve characters.** A safe short key is used AS ITSELF (`build-k-fold-lane-bakery`) and anything else is hashed. `MAX_PLAIN_KEY` was 48 with a comment claiming *"every real site name is under this"* — false for any slug of 49-60 characters, since `cleanSlug` caps at **60**: those were hashed, and a dashboard showed a base36 number where the customer's site name should be. It is 60 now and **the test derives the cap from `cleanSlug`'s own `.slice(0, N)`** rather than restating it, because the two drifting apart is exactly what happened.
- **THE KEYLESS NAME CARRIES NEITHER MARKER, and that is structural rather than tidy.** FNV-1a can answer 0, so `build-h-0` is producible BOTH by a keyless caller and by whichever real slug hashes to zero — one chance in 4.29 billion of a customer's build sharing a working directory with every keyless caller. `build-none` cannot be produced by either branch. What is still forbidden is `undefined`, which takes `getContainer`'s default parameter and restores `cf-singleton-container` invisibly, with every test green.
- **THE `h-` MARKER IS BELT-AND-BRACES TODAY AND SAYS SO rather than being deleted or falsely asserted.** A mutant removing it SURVIVED, and measuring shows why: base36 of a uint32 has the alphabet `0-9a-z` and **no hyphen**, so `build-h-<hash>` can never contain the `k-` every plain name carries. What separates the branches is a property of the OTHER one, which is one edit from changing.
- **`oneAtATime` STAYS AND IS MADE PRECISE RATHER THAN REDUNDANT.** Two builds of one site still share a name, therefore one instance, therefore one working directory — the 2026-07-29 failure. What changes is only that two builds of DIFFERENT sites stop queueing.
- **THE SWEEP FOUND FOUR REAL GAPS AND EVERY ONE WAS MINE.** `keyHash`'s own coercion guard was held by nothing (every coercion case reached it through `laneName`, which had already turned the junk into `""`); nothing asserted a long slug stays legible; nothing asserted the keyless name is unproducible; and nothing asserted the queue's concurrency at all. **18 mutations across three sweeps, 15 caught, 1 proven inert by measurement, 2 comment-only controls that had to survive**, from verified-green isolated baselines.
- 4178 tests. **NOT PROVEN LIVE** — no build has run against it, and what a unit suite structurally cannot show is two real builds occupying two real instances.

## THE CLOCK BOUNDED THE WAIT AND NOT THE SPEND, SO A BUILD BOUGHT A PHOTOGRAPH IT COULD NOT WAIT FOR (2026-08-25)

**Run 37's flagged anomaly, diagnosed off the trace arithmetic alone and fixed.** The owner asked why the site made a space for an image and rendered nothing; the answer is that the photograph was bought, the wait was cut 22.4 seconds in, and the two never met.

- **THE ARITHMETIC IS EXACT AND IT IS THE WHOLE DIAGNOSIS.** Summing the marks before `compile`, the image step began at **517,578ms**; `BUILD_BUDGET_MS` is 780,000, so 262,422 remained; `photoWait` hands the race whatever sits above `PUBLISH_RESERVE_MS` (240,000), which is **22,422ms** — and run 37's `compile` mark is **22,422ms to the millisecond**. That is a timer expiring, not an image model finishing. **A shot has never been observed to land in under ~24.7s**, so it was never going to arrive.
- **WHAT THAT COST, and none of it is the image path malfunctioning.** `done()` read the map at that instant, `applyImages` swept the unmatched `@@IMG:…@@` to the empty string, `SafeImage` drew its placeholder — measured on the served page as `<div role="img" aria-label="A Northkettle three-group machine on a café counter">` inside `aspect-ratio:16/9`, the exact band in the owner's screenshot. Then the shot resolved: **money spent, an orphan permanently holding a slot in the owner's 200-file library, and the site's `og:image` pointing at a photograph on none of its four pages** (`<img>` 0, `data-slot="photo"` 0, measured).
- **AND THE MESSAGE BLAMED THE PROVIDER FOR OUR OWN DEADLINE.** With `made: 0` and a non-zero budget, `imageNote` fell through to *"Couldn't make the photographs this time"* — the image-model-failed sentence, said about a shot that **succeeded** — and it gives the customer nothing to do. `imageNote` exists precisely to stop causes wearing each other's wording, and this was a fifth cause slipping in under the catch-all.
- **SO THE CLOCK IS A THIRD CLAMP ON THE SPEND, beside the credits and the library.** `photoWait` gains `buy`, and `affordable` is zeroed when it is false — so `planImages` returns no shots and nothing is fired. **A third clamp rather than a fourth branch**, deliberately: the machinery for "an allowance of zero" already exists and already sweeps to placeholders, so this needed only the honest number going in.
- **THE COMMENT TREATED THE OLD BEHAVIOUR AS A LAW OF NATURE, and that is the useful part.** It said of `none` that the shots *"have been started and that spend is committed either way"* — an accurate description of what the code did, presented as a given. It is not: **whether to start is ours to decide, from the same reading of the same clock, one subtraction before a penny is spent.**
- **ONE READING, USED TWICE, ASSERTED AS A COUNT.** Asking `photoWait` again at the wait site is asking a clock that has moved in between, so the half that decides to buy and the half that decides to wait could answer differently about one build — which is the shape being fixed, coming back through the door. The guard requires exactly one `photoWait(` in the function.
- **`all` STILL BUYS, and that is not an oversight.** No clock means a caller that set no bound; refusing to buy there would silently stop photographs on every such build — the regression `all` exists to prevent, arriving through the money instead of the wait.
- **`PHOTO_FLOOR_MS` IS 35,000 AND IS CALIBRATED, NOT CHOSEN.** The measured band for a build that landed a photograph is **24.7s–32.6s** (run 35 at 28,089ms sits inside it) against **110ms and 151ms** for builds that bought none; run 37's 22,422 is the timer and is NOT evidence about a shot. Set **above the slowest observed** rather than the fastest, because the two mistakes are asymmetric: being wrong toward not buying costs one placeholder on a site whose owner can **ask again** — and that promise is one the code keeps, checked rather than assumed, since `budgetFor` refuses a revise only when `hasBoughtPhotos` finds a `/u/<slug>/` URL in the STORED pages and a swept placeholder carries none. Being wrong the other way costs money, an orphan and a wrong `og:image`. **n is three, which is small**, and it is the first thing to re-measure once there are more builds to read.
- **`slow` IS SET ONLY WHEN THE CLOCK IS WHAT ZEROED IT, which is `full`'s own discipline** — and the mutual exclusivity falls out of the ordering rather than being restated: a library clamp that already zeroed the budget leaves `beforeClock` at 0, so the clock cannot also claim it. The sentence is the only one of the five whose answer is *"just ask again"*; the other four need money, a deletion or a description.
- 4154 tests (+2), **9/9 mutations as expected** from a verified-green isolated baseline with a comment-only control that had to survive — including the two that read alike from outside: the clamp made inert, and `slow` claiming every zero. **NOT PROVEN LIVE** — no build has run against it, and what a unit suite structurally cannot show is a real shot outrunning a real clock.

## `<main>` HAS NO WIDTH, AND FOR A DAY NOTHING SAID SO (2026-08-25)

**Reported by the owner off a screenshot of run 37: the nav is inset and the page runs edge to edge underneath it.** Three widths on one page — header and footer at `max-w-6xl` with a 24px gutter, the hero's inner div at `max-w-4xl`, and every band below it full-bleed with **no gutter at all**, so the body copy sits against the glass on a phone. The two that look deliberate are the two the model did not write.

- **IT IS THE RUN-34 FINDING REPRODUCED, AND THIS TIME THE CAUSE WAS RE-MEASURED RATHER THAN QUOTED.** `PAGE_RULES` is 42,201 characters and carries **0** `max-w`, **0** `mx-auto`, **0** `px-6` — the two `container` hits are a comment about the build container. `SiteChrome`'s `<main>` is `flex-1 outline-none` by design. The four reference pages DO put `mx-auto max-w-5xl px-6` on all their sections, and they became **data rather than prompt** on 2026-08-24, so the only thing that had ever taught this left and nothing replaced it.
- **THE ONE WIDTH WORD THE MODEL CAN SEE POINTS AT THE WRONG KNOB.** `componentApiFor("site-chrome")` prints `layout?: SiteLayout` with `width?: "contained" | "full"` — and that moves the CHROME. So a model looking for the page's width finds a field that changes the frame instead, which is worse than finding nothing.
- **THE MODEL IS NOT FAILING AT THE PATTERN, IT IS MISSING ONE FACT.** It wrapped the hero correctly — a full-bleed `<section>` with `mx-auto max-w-4xl px-6` inside it, which is the right idiom — and applied it once. Nothing anywhere states what width the site runs at, so there was nothing to be consistent with.
- **THE OBVIOUS FIX IS A CONTAINER ON `<main>` AND IT IS THE WRONG ONE.** Structural and unforgettable — the `safe-image` argument, normally decisive here — and it makes full bleed **inexpressible**: every hero band and colour strip dies platform-wide with no escape hatch, and every existing site is silently re-laid-out on its next publish, which is the "one deploy re-styles no site" rule this repo holds everywhere else.
- **SO IT IS HARD RULE 16, AND `max-w-6xl` IS NAMED RATHER THAN LEFT TO THE MODEL.** Two facts make it a rule instead of a preference: it is the width the chrome already uses, so the page stops disagreeing with its own header; and it resolves through `--container-6xl`, which is what the site-wide content-width axis moves — a hand-picked `max-w-[1100px]` is frozen the way a hardcoded colour is, **which is the argument `## Styling` already makes eight lines earlier about `bg-[#1a1a1a]`.** Same failure, same reasoning, already in the prompt.
- **THE FULL-BLEED EXCEPTION IS IN THE RULE, or the fix kills every hero on the platform.** Keep the bleed on the `<section>`, put the container on a `<div>` inside it. That ratifies what the model already does rather than fighting it.
- **IT IS NOT A `shape` DECISION, AND THAT WAS ASKED AND ANSWERED.** `shape` is per page and optional per page (*"A page you leave out is one the page writer arranges itself"*), so a width living there would let `/` and `/pipeline` disagree — a column that changes as you click is **worse** than the bug being fixed — and the pages nobody described would have no width at all. **What `shape` DOES own is which bands bleed**; rule 16 is the technique for building one. They compose.
- **NO CONDITIONAL FOR `width: "full"`, CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED.** `contained` is the default and `full` only ever arrives on request — and a full-bleed bar over a contained column is an ordinary, deliberate look. The bug is the INVERSE. So `max-w-6xl` is right under both arrangements, and the guard says so, because a rule whose condition the model can get wrong reproduces the bug it replaced.
- **THE FRONTEND PROMPT IS THE HALF THAT MATTERED AND ASSERTING ONLY THE FULL ONE WOULD HAVE BEEN THE GUARD WATCHING THE LAYER BELOW THE BREAK.** A first build has no database, so it reads `frontendRules` output — run 37, where this was measured, was frontend-only. `DATA_RULES` keeps by default, so it lands there as rule **7 of 7**; what the guard catches is somebody naming 16 in that drop list, which would leave the width unstated on exactly the builds that showed the bug.
- **AND ONE ASSERTION OF MINE WAS WEAK BEFORE THE SWEEP EVEN RAN.** The classes appear TWICE in the rule — the instruction and the exception — so a check over the whole rule stays green with the instruction gutted and only the example left, which is an example with nothing it exemplifies. Windowed to the statement.
- **THEN THE SWEEP FOUND BOTH HALVES OF THE PREMISE GUARD VACUOUS, AND BOTH WERE THE PROSE TRAP — IN THE GUARD WRITTEN TO CATCH IT.** `site-chrome.tsx`'s own docstring says *"the page's single `<main>`"*, so `indexOf("<main")` landed on the PROSE at offset 1088 and sliced `<main>` — a tag with no `className`, which passes a "no width here" check whatever the real one carries. And `site-header.tsx` line 89 ARGUES about `max-w-6xl` in a comment, so a bare match found the argument rather than the code and the width could move underneath it. **Two mutants survived: `<main>` gaining a container, and the header's width moving off the one the rule names** — the exact two that make rule 16 a second, disagreeing opinion. Comments blanked length-preservingly now, **with a check that the blanker did not eat the subject too**, since a scan over an over-blanked file reports a clean frame and asserts nothing. Both die on the re-run. **Ninth-plus recorded instance, and the second time in two days it landed inside the guard written for it.**
- **AND MY CONTROL NEVER APPLIED, for the seventh recorded time.** The anchor was `// The site's colours come from its theme` — a line that lives inside a template LITERAL as prompt prose, with no `//` in front of it — so the pattern matched nothing and the sweep had no control at all. **A sweep whose control never applied is a sweep with no control**, which is the state where "everything died" stops being evidence. Re-anchored on a real comment, `grep -cF`'d to 1 before it was believed.
- **+1,319 characters, ~366 tokens on the cached block**, measured rather than estimated (my first figure was ~165 and was wrong by a factor of two).
- 4152 tests (+3), **9/9 mutations as expected on the re-run** from a re-verified isolated baseline with a comment-only control that had to survive — after the first sweep's two survivors and dead control were fixed. **NOT PROVEN LIVE** — no build has generated a page against it.

## RUN 37, PROVEN LIVE: THE STAND-IN COMES DOWN, AND AN UNKNOWN ADDRESS 404s (2026-08-25)

**`https://northgroup-3.gofarther.app/` — the same CRM brief a third time, published in 11m 10s, and the first publish that clears its own placeholder.** `done: true, ok: true, page: "app", at: "pages", total_ms: 669713`, 14 credits, four routes, no database. Served by `x-site-build: mt8movu6-khw003`.

- **THE PROOF IS A PAIR AND NEITHER HALF IS ENOUGH ALONE.** The root answers **200, 11,738 bytes, no mark**; `/no-such-page-xyz` answers **404, 9 bytes**. Against `northgroup-2` — built the same day on the code one commit earlier — which still answers **200, 856 bytes, MARKED** at the identical address. One object different, everything else the same: that is `clearPlaceholder` running on the success path. Checking only the root would pass on a site that still soft-404s; checking only the 404 would pass on a site that never published.
- **THE FULL TRACE**: auth 180 · body 0 · gate 536 · **design 180,874 (in 11,942, out 2,518)** · owner 634 · normalize 0 · **provision 195 (db: 0)** · **schema 0 (tables: 0)** · seed 0 · merge 913 · fonts 362 · gen 168 · **img 333,716** · **compile 22,422** · container 103,352 · og 103 · pages 26,258. Extras: `genMs 333,716` · `tscMs 13,717` · `viteMs 49,084` · `buildMs 103,151` · `renderMs 33,697` · `routesMs 2,250` · `publishMs 26,160`.
- **`img` 333,716 AGAINST RUN 36's 340,277 — 2% apart on the same brief, which is the point.** Run 35 was 619,822 and the day-old entry below reads that swing as the one-sample trend it was. Three runs now: 620k · 340k · 334k. The eight-build median (~390k) still predicts better than any single observation.
- **THE FRONTEND-ONLY SPLIT HELD ON THE HARDEST BRIEF THERE IS.** Measured across all four served pages: `useRows` **0**, `usePublicRows` **0**, `useCreateRow` **0**, `/api/db/` **0**, `<form` **0**, `onSubmit` **0**. A CRM is the shape most likely to reach for a database and it reached for none — `provision` carries `db: 0` and `schema` carries `tables: 0`, the marks that only exist on that path.
- **AND `46bbc4d` IS PROVEN LIVE TOO, on the same run.** The watch printed `(PLACEHOLDER)` for six minutes and said `PUBLISHED` only once the marker was gone AND `done=true` — so the harness that called a running build published on run 36 now reads the body rather than the status code.

**AND ONE PHOTOGRAPH WAS BOUGHT ON A BRIEF WHOSE OWN WORDS ARE "no photographs anywhere", AND IT IS ON NO PAGE.** Flagged, not diagnosed.

- **THE SPAN SAYS IT WAS BOUGHT**: `compile` is 22,422ms against run 36's **151ms** on the identical brief — squarely in the band of builds that DID buy one. The file is real and reachable: `/u/northgroup-3/7e3dc4726414cd27e44e05248446720e.jpg`, `image/jpeg`, 200.
